title: Foundation of the Federal Bar Association Charter Amendments Act of 2025
official_title: An Act to amend title 36, United States Code, to revise the Federal charter for the Foundation of the Federal Bar Association.
likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-57 on December 12, 2025. Passed the Senate on April 30, 2025 and the House on December 1, 2025.
summary: Modernizes the federal charter for the Foundation of the Federal Bar Association, moving governance details to its bylaws and updating standard nonprofit restrictions.
brief: Revises the Title 36 federal charter of the Foundation of the Federal Bar Association.

top_lines.headline: Charter Modernization
subs: Governance and membership rules moved to the bylaws
Principal office no longer fixed in D.C.

items.main: Names the Act the “Foundation of the Federal Bar Association Charter Amendments Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Amends Section 70501 of title 36 by striking subsection (b) and redesignating subsection (c) as subsection (b).
items.detail: Streamlines the corporation's organization provisions in 36 U.S.C. 70501.

items.main: Rewrites Section 70503 so eligibility for membership and the rights and privileges of members are as provided in the bylaws.
items.detail: Strikes the prior subsections (a) and (b) and redesignates subsection (c) as subsection (b); membership terms move to the bylaws except as provided in the chapter.

items.main: Makes the board of directors the governing body, with most details set in the bylaws.
items.detail: Rewrites Section 70504 so the board of directors governs the corporation and may exercise its powers, with the board's responsibilities and the officers' election left to the bylaws. Related amendments move membership eligibility (Section 70503) to the bylaws, allow the principal office to be any U.S. location set by the board (Section 70508, previously the District of Columbia), and update the service-of-process and dissolution rules.

items.main: Updates the restrictions on the Foundation, barring stock, dividends, political activity, lobbying, private inurement, and insider loans.
items.detail: Rewrites Section 70507 of title 36. The corporation may not issue stock or pay dividends; may not use its funds or property for political activity or to influence legislation; may not let income or assets benefit a director, officer, or member (except reasonable compensation and expense reimbursement); may not make loans to insiders; members and individuals are not liable for its obligations; and it may not claim U.S. government approval or authority for its activities.

items.main: Amends Section 70508 so the principal office may be any United States location decided by the board and specified in the bylaws, instead of the District of Columbia.
items.detail: Strikes “the District of Columbia,” and inserts the board-chosen-location language in 36 U.S.C. 70508.

items.main: Rewrites Section 70510 so the corporation must comply with the service-of-process law of the State or District in which it is incorporated.
items.detail: 36 U.S.C. 70510, retitled with a compliance note.

sections.label: Section 8 — Deposit of Assets on Dissolution or Final Liquidation

items.main: Rewrites Section 70512 so on dissolution any remaining assets, after discharging liabilities, are distributed as provided by the board and in compliance with the charter and bylaws.
Provides that the Act's budgetary effects are determined by reference to the latest “Budgetary Effects of PAYGO Legislation” statement for the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act of 2010.
items.detail: Standard PAYGO bookkeeping provision — no substantive effect.

gaps: The bill modernizes the Foundation's charter but does not change its purpose or activities.
It moves governance details from federal law into the Foundation's bylaws, reducing what is fixed in statute.

modified: Federal charter of the Foundation of the Federal Bar Association (title 36, chapter 705) revised — governance and membership moved to bylaws, nonprofit restrictions updated, principal office no longer fixed in D.C.
